extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; creative writers studying narrative structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and constructing narrative fabulas: how information, events, actors, focalization, and temporal/semantic relations are selected, grouped, and interpreted. Useful for narratology students, critics, and writers who want criteria for selecting events/actors and for describing narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense as differential knowledge (reader vs character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense arises from the relationship between what the reader knows and what the character knows; different configurations (reader–character, reader+character, reader–character+, reader+character+) produce different kinds of tension (e.g., riddle/detective story, threat, secret, or no suspense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a question is evoked, analyse which of these knowledge-configurations applies. Examples: detective novel (reader–character), threat (reader+character where character lacks critical knowledge), secret (reader–character+), and when both know the answer there is no suspense. You may further analyse which character knows the answer and through which focalization channel (EF1 or CF2) the reader learns it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization as an overarching determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization has an overarching position with respect to other aspects of narrative; the significance of elements (time, character image, space) cannot be fully viewed unless linked to focalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat focalization as the most important, penetrating, and subtle means of manipulation. Include focalization in analyses (e.g., to reveal ideology in newspaper reports) rather than restricting investigation to semantic content analysis alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabula composed of objects (stable) and processes (changeable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The material constituting a fabula can be divided into stable elements (objects: actors, locations, things) and changeable elements (processes: events). Both are indispensable for constructing a fabula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse fabula elements structurally: identify objects and processes and how they interrelate. This structuralist approach applies beyond literature to films, theatre, news reports, and real-world event series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event definition: transition between states caused/experienced by actors
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is defined as the transition from one state to another state, caused or experienced by actors — i.e., a process, an alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Event-identification begins by trying to establish which sentences represent events. This is interpretive: consider context and relations rather than isolated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event selection criterion — Change (condition vs change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between sentences that state a condition and those that describe a change (e.g., 'John is ill' vs 'John falls ill'). Events should indicate change; isolated conditions need contextual series to function as events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surrounding text to decide whether a fact functions as a change/event. Linguistic form (presence of an action verb) is indicative but not decisive; restating text to make implicit relations explicit (e.g., adding 'stop') can aid selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event selection criterion — Choice / functional events (Barthes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional events open a choice between possibilities, realize a choice, or reveal the results; once a choice is made, it determines subsequent course of events in the fabula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a segment makes a real causal/choiceful difference to later events (examples: turning left that results in arriving in time vs being run down while crossing). Even spectacular occurrences are non-functional if unrelated to the fabula's development. Use relevance to subsequent events as the test for functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event selection criterion — Confrontation (two actors + one action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every phase of the fabula (every functional event) has three components: two actors and one action — logically: two arguments and one predicate; linguistically: subject–predicate–(direct) object where both subject and direct object must be actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the second actor is not explicitly named, inferability from context can permit classification as a functional event (e.g., 'Liz writes a letter' implies a recipient). Beware actions whose objects are non-actors (e.g., killing a fly vs killing a woman) — contextual interpretation determines whether the object functions as an actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of linguistic reformulation to reveal events
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit relations can often be made explicit by restating sentences (e.g., introducing verbs like 'stop') so that events and causal relations become clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological step, reformulate sentences to test whether an implicit event relation exists; this aids preliminary selection of events but is an interpretive move and should be documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model comparison: map concrete fabula onto abstract templates (Bremond)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a concrete series of events with an abstract model (e.g., Bremond's model) to describe fabula structure precisely, making fits and deviations visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abstract models to reveal structure and meaningful deviations, but do not force the text into a model. The confrontation aims to make the text-specific structure legible and to highlight interpretive differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate logical and conventional restrictions in narrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative rules derive from logical restrictions (e.g., effect succeeds cause) and conventional restrictions (genre/cultural norms that shape plausibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying abstract models, be aware that conventional restrictions vary historically and culturally; test assumptions rather than treating conventions as universal norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative cycle phases: possibility, realization (event), and result
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fabula can be analysed as cycles of three phases — possibility (virtuality), event (realization), and result (conclusion) — though any phase can be absent (unrealized possibility, inconclusive result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cycle to chart alternatives (e.g., preparing for an exam vs not preparing; passing vs failing). Recognize premature cycle completion, negative conclusions that may recommence cycles, and that phases are not always explicit in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary series, succession and embedding of processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary series (virtuality → realization → result) can be combined: processes may succeed one another or be embedded (one process opening another). Embedded series can be more important than primary series and shape fabula style (e.g., determinism, fatalism, minimalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map sequences and embeddings to understand causality and thematic emphasis. Note how embedding can shift prominence and interpretative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic labelling of processes (improvement vs deterioration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply semantic labels to events (e.g., fulfilment of the task, intervention of allies, elimination of the opponent, negotiation, attack, satisfaction) to compare and abstract fabula structures; processes are broadly categorizable as improvement or deterioration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label events at an abstract semantic level to facilitate cross-text comparison. Be explicit about interpretive choices (e.g., whether a specific event counts as 'satisfaction' or 'punishment').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterioration process types (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes of deterioration can be typified (e.g., the misstep; the creation of an obligation; the sacrifice; the endured attack; the endured punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sub-classes to specify forms of deterioration; apply further concrete specifications when comparing narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other structuring principles: actor-identity, confrontation nature, time, and location
rubrics_metrics.description: Events can be grouped by: (1) identity of the actors (segmenting fabula by which actor is subject), (2) nature of confrontation (verbal, mental, bodily; success/failure), (3) temporal relations (simultaneity vs succession), and (4) location oppositions (inside–outside, city–country, above–below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine these principles to build explicit, intersubjective models of structure relevant to your research question. Avoid irrelevant comparisons (e.g., contrasting weather occurrences when weather is not meaningfully connected to events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor selection: functional vs non-functional actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Select actors who participate in functional events (those who cause or undergo events that shape the fabula); actors who perform non-functional actions may be left out of structural analysis though they can carry cultural/social meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base actor selection on prior event analysis when possible. If skipping event analysis, use intuitive summaries or ask multiple readers to produce summaries and use their common elements to avoid circularity and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actantial classification (Greimas) — actors by relation to the aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify actors into actants: classes of actors sharing a relation to the fabula's teleology (aspiration towards gain or avoidance of loss); functions derive from these teleological relations (wish/fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use actantial roles to generalize actor functions across fabulas; treat actants as structural categories that relate to the story's telos rather than as individual character descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit the link between data selection and analytic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures are formed by the investigator based on selected events combined with other data; the relationship between the data and analytic operations must be explicit and relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document why certain events/actors/relations were selected and how they inform the structural claims. This increases intersubjective understandability and prevents arbitrary or hidden analytic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse which character knows what and through which focalization channel
rubrics_metrics.description: When questions are evoked in the narrative, specify which character knows the answer and through which focalizer (external/character focalization channels like EF1 or CF2) the reader obtains information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map knowledge-distribution across characters and mark the channels by which the reader is informed; this refines suspense/secret analyses and ties focalization to information flow.
